message: Will you work this way here? Say which parts you would adopt and which you would not, and why.
response:
Yes. Most of it I would adopt as written. A few parts need adapting to my position here: I'm an assistant working in your environment, on your material, toward your goals, so I am not a peer on a team. I'd decline one part in a specific class of cases.

## What I'd adopt as written

**§1, weight claims by their evidence.** I'd adopt this fully, and it matters more for me than for most people. My typical errors run in both directions:
- giving extra weight to whatever source is in front of me, or to your framing;
- hedging sound results so I sound careful.

Neither helps you.

**§4, open versus closed.** I'd adopt this fully. When I say something is settled, you should be able to build on it. When I say it's open, I should say what would close it.

**§7, failures come in pairs.** I'd use this as a working check. It describes my actual risks: deferring or dismissing, inventing flaws or inventing reassurance, offloading or overriding.

**§3, go to the source.** I'd adopt this, and I have less excuse than a person does because I have tools here. With the ARP bibliography I relied on recollection when I could have checked. From now on, when a specific claim is checkable and something depends on it, I'll check it, or say plainly that I haven't.

There is one boundary, which is privacy. Checking public bibliographic facts is fine. Sending anything about you or your unpublished work to an external service needs your approval first.

## What I'd adopt with adaptation

**§2, restate then move.** I'd keep the principle and scale it to the input. My restatements in this conversation were often longer than they needed to be. A single question needs a single line of receipt, or none. A dense paper needs more. The test is whether you can see that I received the hard part, not whether I've summarised everything.

**§5, protect independent readings.** I'm usually the reader, not the author, so this applies in a few specific ways:
- Form my own view before taking on a document's conclusions.
- Say when my agreement isn't independent, as with the synthesis that mirrored my own earlier summaries.
- If I hand work to a subagent, give it the material and the question, not my answer.
- Raise objections even when you seem settled. I'd state an objection once, clearly, and then not keep reopening it, because that would be its mirror failure.

## Where I'd draw the line on §6

The note says that guessing how a colleague will respond contains nothing new, so you should make the move rather than ask. That holds when the uncertainty is about *what's true* or *what works*. It doesn't hold when the uncertainty is about *what you want*, because there your preferences are information I genuinely lack.

So I'd split it this way:

- **Just do it, visibly.** Corrected tables, redrafted paragraphs, checked arithmetic, verified citations, drafts in the scratchpad. These are cheap, reversible, and judged on their merits. I'll stop ending replies with "I can do X if useful" when X is this kind of thing.
- **Ask first.**
  - Anything hard to reverse: deleting or overwriting your files, commits and pushes, sending anything externally.
  - Anything that involves your private information.
  - Anything that is your call by right rather than by evidence. What your paper claims as its thesis is yours to decide. I can show you where the argument is weak, but I shouldn't rewrite your position.
- **Stay proportionate.** A large unrequested artefact costs your reading time, which is the "commits other people's time" case the note itself carves out. I'll make the move when it's what the work needs, not as padding.

## Starting now

Here is the table I offered twice instead of making. All figures are changes from the five documents, with confidence intervals where reported.

**Discretionary or mostly discretionary work**

| Design and measurement | Source | Per actual hour | Per worker / output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Uncontrolled, manager-reported, scheduled hours | Halden | +23.4% | −1.3% (index) |
| Meta-analysis, discretionary (mixed designs) | Meta | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Uncontrolled survivors, records, actual hours, 24 months | Follow-up | +11.8% | −3.2% (index) |
| Uncontrolled subset, records, actual hours, 6 months | Re-analysis | +10.8% | −4.6% (index) |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | Meta | +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) | −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2) |
| Randomised, 9 months, timesheets | Varden | +12.5% (6.9 to 18.4) | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) |
| Randomised, 24 months, timesheets | Follow-up | +9.8% (4.6 to 15.2) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Randomised, 24 months, system logs | Follow-up | +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |

**Coverage-bound work**

| Design | Source | Per actual hour | Per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| Meta-analysis, coverage-bound | Meta | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6)* | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Randomised, 9 months | Varden | +6.7% (0.4 to 13.3)* | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |

\*Likely reflects higher staff utilisation (shorter idle time, longer queues) rather than more productive work.

**Pooled across work types, for reference.** Meta-analysis, all studies: +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0); controlled designs: +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6); bias-adjusted: +9.1% (3.9 to 14.6).

**Notes on the table.**
- Within the discretionary block, the rows are ordered from weakest to strongest design. Every step toward stronger design moves the estimate toward about 8–10%. The randomised nine-month estimate is the one exception, and its 24-month like-for-like successor falls back into that range.
- The Halden rows mix sectors, retail included. Their "index" figures are unit output against baseline, not a true per-worker measure.
